1.pericope_label: When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation: of the male from twenty years old unto sixty, fifty shekels of silver

schools.summary: Gill marks the seam in the book, since the body of laws in the preceding chapter seems by its close to have been finished, and what is added here concerns vows, which a man was not obliged to make but did of his own freewill and good pleasure. He notes that the address to the children of Israel concerns them only, the Jewish writers taking the phrase to exclude Gentiles, and that the estimation was not left to be made by the man who vowed or by the priest at either one's pleasure, but according to the rules that follow, in proportion to the age of the person estimated. Calvin sets out the framework of the whole chapter, which shows in what manner and at what price what has once been offered is to be redeemed, supposing that the vows cannot conveniently be paid. He distinguishes two modes of consecration among the ancient people, the ban, whose Hebrew name is equivalent to destruction or desolation, and the ordinary devoting for the use of the temple and other exercises of religion. The first might be made of unclean animals and other unholy things, as in the case of the city of Jericho and similar instances; but it was not properly allowable to make vows except of a clean man or animal, or of something else that might be appropriated to the service of God, so that of their flocks they vowed goats and sheep and of their herds oxen or calves.

Henry treats the chapter as part of the law concerning singular vows, extraordinary ones which, though God did not expressly insist on them, he would be well pleased with if they were consistent with and conformable to the general precepts. From this he draws a rule: we should not only ask what we must do, but what we may do, for the glory and honour of God; as the liberal devises liberal things, so the pious devises pious things, and the enlarged heart would willingly do something extraordinary in the service of so good a Master. When we receive or expect some singular mercy, he adds, it is good to honour God with some singular vow. On the case of persons vowed by such a vow he supposes a man consecrating himself, or a child, to the service of the tabernacle, to be employed there in some inferior office, such as sweeping the floor, carrying out ashes or running errands.

Ellicott observes that the section is introduced with the formula which indicates a separate divine communication, and that since sundry allusions are made throughout the book to vows, legally acknowledging the ancient practice of votive offerings, a code pre-eminently designed to uphold the holiness of the sanctuary and its sacrifices, and of the priests and the people, would be incomplete without defining the nature and obligation of these self-imposed sacrifices. On the phrase for making a vow he reports the interpretation that obtained during the second Temple, that it denotes pronouncing a vow, which the ancient Chaldee versions render distinctly pronouncing, so that no vow mentally made or conceived was deemed binding; the form of the vow is nowhere given in the Bible, its wording being left, like many other points of detail, to the administrators of the law, who divided vows into positive and negative. On the valuation he notes that the estimation begins with the male as the most important person and takes special notice of his age, the years specified being the prime of life, and that a man is rated not according to his rank or position but according to the value of his services, the sum falling alike on rich and poor. Keil corrects the verb, which does not mean to dedicate or set apart a vow but to make a special one, and gives the whole table of prices, adding that it was regulated by capacity and vigour of life, the female being appraised at half the male amount as the weaker vessel.

Clarke opens with a summary of the chapter and then explains the obscure second verse, paraphrasing it as meaning that he who has vowed or consecrated a living creature, whether man or beast, shall, if he wishes to redeem it, ransom it according to the priest's estimation; for the priest shall judge of the properties, qualifications and age of the person or beast, and of the circumstances of the person who has vowed it, and shall regulate the value accordingly, the money being put into his hands for the service of the sanctuary. He cites Ainsworth that a vow is a religious promise made unto the Lord, for the most part with prayer, and paid with thanksgiving. He also reduces the first valuation to the sterling of his own day. Wesley calls this an eminent or hard vow, not concerning things, which was customary, but concerning persons, which was unusual and difficult. He recalls instances of those who devoted themselves or their children, whether more strictly, as the Nazarites and the Levites, for whom no redemption was admitted since they were in person to perform the service to which they were devoted, or more largely, as some not of that tribe who through zeal to God, or to obtain his help, devoted themselves or their children in some subserviency; and since too great a number so dedicated might be burdensome to the sanctuary, the estimation was provided. Of the prime years he says they are the best time for strength and service and therefore prized at the highest rate.

debates: What kind of vow is meant: Wesley takes it of persons rather than things and calls it unusual and difficult, Keil corrects the verb to mean the making of a special vow rather than the setting apart of one, Ellicott reports the second-Temple rule that it must be distinctly pronounced and that no mental vow bound, and Calvin sets it against the ban, which could fall on unclean things while a vow could not

On what principle the valuation is fixed: Keil says it followed capacity and vigour of life, with the female at half the male rate as the weaker vessel, Ellicott that a man was rated by the value of his services and not by rank or position, and Wesley that the prime years were prized highest as the best time for strength and service; Ellicott and Gill agree that the sum was fixed and not left to the parties

Why an estimation was needed at all: Wesley grounds it on the burden to the sanctuary of too many dedicated persons, Clarke on the priest's judgment of the circumstances of the man who vowed, Calvin on the case where the vow cannot conveniently be paid, and Henry on the voluntary and extraordinary character of such vows
outliers: Henry says that when we receive or expect some singular mercy it is good to honour God with some singular vow
Gill notes that the Jewish writers took the address to the children of Israel as excluding Gentiles
Clarke cites Ainsworth that a vow is a religious promise made with prayer and paid with thanksgiving
Calvin observes that the Hebrew name of the ban is equivalent to destruction or desolation

4.pericope_label: If it be a female, thirty shekels; from five years old to twenty, twenty and ten; from a month to five years, five and three; from sixty and above, fifteen and ten

schools.summary: Gill keeps the ages exact, noting that the female of the first class is of the same age as the male, full twenty and not more than sixty. On the class of children he is careful about who does the vowing: it is not that one of five years old is supposed to vow or to make an estimation, but that a grown person says the estimation of this little one, who is five years of age, be upon me, and such a one was then bound to pay the value. The same holds of the youngest class, where a man devotes his child within that age and says the estimation of this my son or my daughter be upon me, and then pays the value directed; and for one under a month old no estimation was to be made at all, the Jewish rule being that one less than a month old may be vowed but not estimated. Of the oldest class he gives the plain reason for the fall in price, that at sixty a man is almost past his labour and it is high time to leave off business. The last case he takes of one so poor that he is not able to pay the value set upon him according to the rules already given.

Ellicott explains the woman's lower rate from her being the weaker vessel whose labour is of less value, and adds that thirty shekels was the value of a slave and the price at which Christ was sold, and that it has been supposed Jephthah might under this provision have redeemed the daughter he unwittingly vowed, though he refers the reader to the later law of the devoted thing. From the mention of a child of five he draws an argument about the nature of these vows: since a vow involving the payment of a considerable sum on the part of a child was of no force, the case contemplated must be that of a father or mother vowing a male child to the Lord, or of another person taking upon himself to pay the value of such a child to the sanctuary, and the next verse makes this still more manifest; the formula used during the second Temple was, Behold the estimation of this my boy, or this my girl, or of that boy or that girl, be upon me. He ranks the old man next in value to the child, and observes that the old woman is estimated at exactly the same value as the girl from five to twenty, so that the disproportion between the sexes is not the same in old age as in youth; the authorities of the second Temple accounted for this by the adage that an old man in the house is always in the way while an old woman is a treasure who manages all the household affairs. On the poor man he sets out the procedure, that he presents himself before the priest, who examines his circumstances and taxes him accordingly, the minimum during the second Temple being one shekel.

Clarke reduces every figure in the table to the sterling of his own day and gives a reason for each ratio. The woman at the same age might be redeemed for a little more than half the value of the man, for the obvious reason that a woman, if employed, could not be of so much use in the service of the sanctuary and was therefore of much less value. The boy and girl of the youngest class, being both in comparative infancy, were nearly of an equal value; and the old man and old woman, being nearly past labour, were likewise nearly of equal value, which he notes is about the same ratio as that of the children and for the same reason. He also observes that none were vowed under a month old, and that the firstborn, being always considered the Lord's property already, could not be vowed at all. Wesley states the woman's case in a line, that thirty shekels is less than the man's price because she is inferior to him both in strength and serviceableness. On the children he notes the age at which they might be vowed by their parents, though not by themselves, and holds that the children were obliged by their parents' vow, which he does not find strange considering the parents' right to dispose of their children so far as it is not contrary to the mind of God. The last verse he takes of the man not able to pay the price which the rules require of him.

debates: Why the female rate is lower: Clarke grounds it on her being of less use in the service of the sanctuary, Wesley on her being inferior in strength and serviceableness, and Ellicott on her being the weaker vessel whose labour is of less value; none of them makes it a judgment of worth rather than of service

Who makes the vow when a child is valued: Ellicott argues from the age of five that the vow must be a parent's or another's and not the child's, since a child could not bind himself to such a payment, Gill says the same by supplying the formula in which a grown person takes the estimation upon himself, and Wesley grounds the child's obligation on the parents' right to dispose of their children so far as it is not contrary to the mind of God

Why the sexes are nearer in price at the two ends of life: Clarke says infancy and old age alike are nearly past or not yet come to labour, so the ratio is the same in both, while Ellicott notices that the old woman is priced exactly at the girl's rate and reports the second-Temple adage that an old man in the house is in the way while an old woman manages all its affairs
outliers: Ellicott notes that thirty shekels was the price of a slave and the sum for which Christ was sold
Ellicott suggests that Jephthah might have redeemed his daughter under this provision, while pointing to the later law of the devoted thing
Gill reports the Jewish rule that a child less than a month old may be vowed but not estimated
Ellicott records that a debtor's goods were seized for unpaid vows, but that the bailiffs had to leave a mechanic two sets of tools

9.pericope_label: If it be a beast whereof men bring an offering, it shall be holy; he shall not alter it nor change it; but an unclean beast the priest shall value, and the fifth part added

schools.summary: Gill defines the first class as creatures of the kind used in sacrifice to the Lord, such as bullocks, sheep, goats, rams and lambs. On the two verbs of the prohibition he reports that some think they signify the same thing, but that Abarbinel makes them different: to alter is to put one of another kind in its place, as one of the herd for one of the flock or the contrary, and to change is to put one of the same kind. Of the unclean beast he says any creature is meant except a dog, whose price was not to be brought into the house of the Lord, though some, and Jarchi among them, understand the phrase even of animals with blemishes on them and so unfit to be offered. The priest, he adds, was to put a price on the beast according to its worth as it appeared to him, and the redemption clause concerns the owner who devoted it, if he is determined to have it again at any rate. Calvin summarises the section as treating in the second place of brute animals, which God commands to be sacrificed if they are suitable and does not suffer the vow to be altered, while laying down a rule of redemption for the imperfect and the unclean. He then raises a question the others pass over, how it can be allowable to vow what God had forbidden to be offered to him and prohibited from being brought into the temple as unclean, since anyone who thought to sacrifice such an animal would have his superstition rejected and would need expiation.

Ellicott identifies the first class as the sacrificial quadrupeds, bullocks, sheep and goats, and explains that being holy here means the beast must not be redeemed at all: such animals were delivered to the sanctuary, where the priests sold them to those Israelites who required sacrifices for the altar, and the money was spent on the maintenance of the service. On the prohibition he says the identical animal vowed is to be delivered and no change whatever permitted, not even the substitution of a better for an inferior, the stress being shown by the use of two verbs of the same import, and that if the exchange is made both animals alike are holy and must go to the sanctuary. The unclean beast he takes of an animal outside the three sacrificial kinds, while reporting that the authorities of the second Temple understood the phrase of defective sacrificial animals, oxen and sheep and goats with blemishes which had become unlawful for the altar. On the valuation he says the priest estimates by the condition of the animal, whatever it may be, and he draws out a distinction the text leaves implicit, that the estimate was meant for anyone who wished to purchase, the man who vowed it not excluded, but that the former owner alone pays a fifth above the price, probably as a fine for taking back what he promised. Keil gives the same rule and adds that an unclean beast, an ass for example, was valued between good and bad, at a medium price, and that the fifth is a kind of compensation.

Clarke draws the principle out of the prohibition: whatever was consecrated to God by a vow, or by a purpose of heart, was considered from that moment as the Lord's property, so that to change it was impiety and to withhold it sacrilege. He then turns the law upon the reader, asking whether he has ever dedicated himself or any part of his property to the service of his Maker, whether he has paid his vows or altered his purpose and changed his offering, whether God has received from his hands a bad in place of a good, and whether he was not himself vowed and consecrated to God in his baptism, so that those vows are still upon him. Of the added fifth he says it was probably intended to prevent rash vows and covetous redemptions, since the priest alone was to value the thing and a fifth had to be added by whoever wished to redeem it; if the priest valued it at forty shekels, the former owner had to give forty-eight. Wesley takes the first clause of a clean beast and holds that being holy means consecrated to God either to be sacrificed or to be given to the priest, according to the manner of the vow and the intention of the man who vowed. The two verbs he treats as one thing said more emphatically, and gives two reasons for the strictness, that God would preserve the reverence of consecrated things and not have them alienated, and that men might otherwise exchange under that pretence for the worse; the forfeiting of both animals he calls a just penalty for levity in such weighty matters.

debates: Whether the two verbs of the prohibition differ: Gill reports Abarbinel distinguishing them, the one an exchange across kinds and the other within a kind, while Wesley and Ellicott treat them as the same thing said twice for emphasis, Ellicott finding in the repetition the measure of the stress laid on the rule

What an unclean beast means here: Ellicott and Keil take it of animals outside the sacrificial kinds, an ass for instance, while Ellicott also reports and Gill repeats the second-Temple reading that blemished oxen and sheep and goats are meant, animals that had become unlawful for the altar

Why a fifth is added on redemption: Clarke thinks it a check on rash vows and covetous redemptions, Ellicott a fine for taking back what was promised, since any other purchaser paid only the valuation, and Keil a kind of compensation for recovering the animal vowed
outliers: Ellicott explains that beasts fit for the altar were sold by the priests to Israelites needing sacrifices, the money maintaining the service
Calvin asks how an unclean animal could lawfully be vowed at all when it could not be offered
Clarke turns the law on the reader, asking whether the vows of his baptism are still upon him
Keil says the unclean beast was to be valued between good and bad, at a medium price

14.pericope_label: When a man shall sanctify his house to be holy unto the LORD, the priest shall estimate it; and if he will redeem it, he shall add the fifth part of the money

schools.summary: Gill takes the sanctifying as setting the house apart for sacred service and devoting it to holy uses, so that it may be sold and the money laid out in sacrifices and the repairs of the temple, and he notes that other goods are comprehended under the same head. He supplies the Jewish rules that guarded other people's claims: a wife could not demand her dowry out of what had been sanctified, nor a creditor his debt, though the man might redeem on condition that he gave the dowry to the wife and the debt to the creditor; and whether he sanctified or estimated his goods, he had no power over his wife's or his children's clothes. On the redemption he says the house might be redeemed either by another paying the price the priest had set or by the original owner paying a fifth part more, and that this held alike of houses in walled cities and in villages; he cites Maimonides for what followed, that a redeemed house in a walled city became absolutely the redeemer's if it stayed in his possession twelve months, while one in the villages returned to its owner at the jubilee. Calvin treats this as a third kind of vow, the consecration of houses and lands, under which an alternative is appointed so that religion may not be despised and yet the just possessors not be driven from their houses nor the lands rendered useless for want of cultivation.

Henry treats the passage as the law concerning real estates dedicated to God by a singular vow. If a man in his zeal for the honour of God sanctified his house, the house was to be valued by the priest and the money got by the sale converted to the use of the sanctuary, which by degrees came to be greatly enriched with dedicated things. If the owner was inclined to redeem it himself, he must not have it so cheap as another would, but must add a fifth part to the price, for he should have considered before he vowed. Out of that Henry draws the comparison that gives the section its point: to the man who was necessitous God would abate the estimation, as the earlier law of the poor man provided, but to the man who was fickle and humoursome, whose second thoughts inclined more to the world and his secular interest than his first, God would rise in the price. He closes by turning the law to present use, that there is a way of sanctifying our houses to be holy unto the Lord without either selling them or buying them back again.

Ellicott says the house devoted by a vow has to be sold and the money used by the authorities for the maintenance and repair of the sanctuary, unless it is required as a dwelling for the priests or for some other purpose connected with the duties of the Temple, and that the sale can take place only after the priest has carefully examined the house, ascertained its condition and fixed its value, at which price anyone may then buy it. He reports that the authorities during the second Temple interpreted the word house to mean not only the building itself but anything belonging to it or any article of furniture in it, which the owner might vow to the sanctuary separately, and that from the phrase his house they concluded the property must be absolutely his own and at his exclusive disposal. On the redemption he notes that the fifth falls only on the former owner, or, by the practice of the second Temple, on his son, wife or nearest of kin, everyone else paying the bare valuation, and that the reason is the same as in the case of animals, namely the taking back of a thing once promised to the Lord. Keil says the rules for a vowed house were those already given for unclean cattle, and expressly rejects Knobel's supposition that the man who vowed had to pay the valuation price if he did not wish to redeem it, calling it quite groundless, since the house that was not redeemed was simply sold for the good of the sanctuary.

Clarke gives a reading of the transaction that none of the others adopt, that what went towards the repairs of the tabernacle, which was the house of the Lord, was the yearly rent of the house once it had been consecrated, rather than the price fetched by selling it outright. Wesley confines the sanctifying to that which is done by a vow, since it is of that way and manner of sanctification that the whole chapter speaks; and on the added fifth he observes that the owner might the better bear it because the priests usually put a moderate rate upon the thing in the first place, so that the surcharge fell on a valuation already gentle.

debates: What the sanctuary actually received: Gill, Henry, Ellicott and Keil all take it that the house was sold and the price went to the sanctuary, Ellicott allowing that it might instead be kept as a dwelling for the priests, while Clarke alone speaks of the yearly rent of the consecrated house going to the repairs of the tabernacle

What happened if the owner did not redeem: Keil names and rejects Knobel's view that the man who vowed had then to pay the valuation price, holding instead that the house was simply sold for the sanctuary's benefit

Why the owner pays more than a stranger: Ellicott makes it the same fine as with the animals, for taking back what was promised, Wesley softens it by noting that the priests valued moderately to begin with, and Henry turns it into a moral contrast with the earlier abatement for the poor, since God abates for the necessitous and raises the price for the fickle
outliers: Ellicott reports that the second-Temple rule extended the right of redemption to the man's son, wife or nearest of kin
Gill records that a sanctified house could not be reached by a wife's dowry or a creditor's debt, though redemption required both to be paid

Calvin allows that superstitious prayers were sometimes mixed with these vows, as if favour could be bought by a bargain with God, and that God bore with the error rather than abolish what was laudable
Henry says there is a way of sanctifying our houses without either selling them or buying them back

16.pericope_label: If a man shall sanctify some part of a field of his possession, thy estimation shall be according to the seed thereof; and if he will not redeem it, the field shall be the priest’s

schools.summary: Gill takes the field of his possession as that enjoyed by inheritance from his father, distinguished from a field of the man's own purchase, and explains why only part might be devoted: partly that he might have something to live upon or to improve for a livelihood for himself and his family, and partly that estates might not be alienated entirely from the families and tribes to which they belonged. On the jubilee reckoning he cites Aben Ezra for the case of a field sanctified in the jubilee year itself, while it is current or when it is just past, and Jarchi for the case where a purchaser comes forward as soon as the field is devoted and the priest has valued it; the second case he takes of a sanctifying some years after the jubilee, it may be half way towards another or nearer. Of the man who redeems he says he is one desirous of the field and determined upon it at any rate, repenting that he parted with it in this manner; and of the man who does not redeem, that he does not care to give the settled price with the fifth part besides, but chooses rather that it should be disposed of for the uses he devoted it to. When the field goes out at the jubilee, he notes, it goes out of the hand of the man who bought it.

Ellicott says the words some part are implied in the Hebrew construction, since no man was allowed to vow the whole of his estates to the sanctuary, and that the field meant is one inherited from his forefathers and forming part of his inalienable patrimony, as distinguished from a field acquired by his own purchase. On the calendar he states the rule exactly: the valuation of fifty shekels applies only if the vow is made immediately after the expiration of a jubilee year, when the period covered by the estimate is forty-nine years; if the vow is made later, the priest values the field by the number of years remaining to the next jubilee, the years already elapsed being deducted and so many shekels taken off the original sum. He observes that the low value fixed per acre was designed so that the field should be redeemed by the man himself, and that the legislation of the second Temple extended the right of redemption to his wife and his heirs, the family paying as usual a fifth above the valuation. If the man foregoes that privilege he shows no desire to perpetuate his family name, and if he then sells to another the field he has vowed he adds fraud to it; the field accordingly does not revert to him at the jubilee but becomes God's property like all devoted things. Keil gives the same reckoning, works out the size of an omer from the ephah and from the calculation of Thenius, and notes that the possession falls to the priest.

Clarke says the words some part, though not in the text, are generally allowed to be supplied there, since it was not lawful for a man to vow his whole estate and thus make his family beggars in order to enrich the Lord's sanctuary, which God would not permit. He reports the rabbinic rule that the land, whether good or bad, was valued at forty-eight shekels for all the years of the jubilee, provided the field was large enough to sow a homer of barley, and he distinguishes the homer from the other measure of similar name. Of the field that is not redeemed he says it becomes a thing under the ban, so devoted to God as never more to be capable of being redeemed. Wesley likewise takes the field as one held by inheritance, particular direction being given elsewhere about purchased lands, and gives his own reason for the restriction to part, that by vowing away all his possessions a man disabled himself from the performance of divers duties and made himself burdensome to his brethren. The estimate he explains as going by the quantity and quality of the land, which is known by the quantity of seed it can receive and return; the abatement is more or less as the years are more or fewer. He reads the closing case as the priest offering the field first to the man who vowed it and, on his refusal, selling it to another, after which the man for ever loses the benefit of redemption; and he answers the objection that giving the possession to the priests conflicts with the law that they should have no inheritance in the land, since that was spoken of the tribe in general with reference to the first division of the land.

debates: Why only part of a field may be vowed: Clarke says a man might not make his family beggars to enrich the sanctuary and that God would not permit it, Gill adds that estates were not to be alienated from their families and tribes, Wesley that a man would thereby disable himself from other duties and become burdensome to his brethren, while Ellicott rests it on the Hebrew construction itself

How the field is valued: Keil and Wesley take the estimate from the measure of seed the ground receives, Keil computing the size of the omer from the ephah, while Clarke reports the rabbinic figure of forty-eight shekels for the whole jubilee period on a field sown with a homer of barley

What the failure to redeem shows and costs: Ellicott reads it as a want of desire to perpetuate the family name, compounded by fraud if the vowed field is then sold, Wesley as a forfeiture following the priest's offer and the man's refusal, and Gill more mildly as a preference that the field be used for the purpose it was devoted to
outliers: Wesley answers the objection that giving vowed land to the priests conflicts with the law that Levi should have no inheritance
Ellicott says the per-acre price was set low on purpose, so that the owner would redeem
Clarke calls the unredeemed field a thing under the ban, never again capable of redemption
Gill describes the redeeming owner as one repenting that he parted with the field in this manner

22.pericope_label: If a man sanctify a field which he hath bought, the priest shall reckon the worth unto the year of jubile; and in the jubile the field shall return unto him of whom it was bought

schools.summary: Gill describes the purchased field as one bought with the man's own money from some person in poverty and distress who was obliged to sell it, and which according to the former law returned to the original proprietor in the year of jubilee. On the reckoning he says the priest was to estimate the field of purchase that had been sanctified and to set a price upon it according to the best of his judgment, giving it to the person who sanctified it or to whoever would redeem it, the estimate being made according to the number of years remaining to the jubilee. On the reversion he is careful to exclude two claimants who might have been expected: the field returns neither to the man who sanctified it, whether he redeemed it or not, nor to anyone who bought it from the treasurer of the temple after it had been sanctified, but to the original proprietor and owner from whom the man who vowed it had bought it. On the shekel of the sanctuary he guards the phrase against a misunderstanding: it does not mean that there was a shekel in the sanctuary different from the common one, since every shekel ought to have been as that was, of the full weight and worth of it; the point is that the estimation was to be made according to such a shekel and the money paid in full weight.

Ellicott explains why the case must differ, since a field acquired by purchase is the buyer's only until the next jubilee, when it reverts to its original owner, so that what is vowed is in effect a lease. The rule accordingly changes: the man who vows such a field does not pay the low rate fixed for a family inheritance, but the priest values it in proportion to the number of crops it will produce up to the year of jubilee, in the same way as fields are valued in ordinary purchases. Two differences follow, that this valuation had to be paid all at once and without the additional fifth part of its value, whereas the man who vowed an hereditary field had the advantage of paying the smaller sum by yearly instalments. On the reversion he refers to the standing law of the jubilee, by which the field thus vowed did not return to the purchaser but to the hereditary owner from whom the man who vowed it had bought it. On the last verse he gives the reason for the standard: since the proceeds of these vows were devoted to the maintenance and repair of the sanctuary, all the valuations were to be made and paid according to the standard weight of the sanctuary shekel. Keil records that the estimation was to be given in that day as a holy thing to the Lord, and that all valuations were to be made by that shekel.

Wesley marks the distinction from the other side, glossing the possession of the preceding verses as a man's patrimony or inheritance, so that the purchased field stands apart from it. The estimation he takes as the price which Moses had by divine direction been appointed to set in such cases, and the term as covering only the space between the making of the vow and the year of jubilee, since the man had no right to the field for any longer time, as the next verse shows. The sum paid he calls a holy thing, as being that which is consecrated to God instead of the land redeemed by it. Clarke has only the last verse, where he explains the shekel of the sanctuary as a standard shekel, the standard being kept in the sanctuary in order to try and regulate all the weights in the land by it.

debates: Why a purchased field is valued differently from an inherited one: Ellicott grounds it on the buyer holding only until the jubilee, so that the priest values by the crops remaining rather than by the fixed rate, and adds that the sum falls due at once and without the fifth, while Wesley rests the same limit on the man's having no right to the field beyond that year

Who receives the field at the jubilee: Gill excludes both the man who sanctified it and any later purchaser from the temple treasurer, and Ellicott likewise refers it to the hereditary owner under the standing law, so that the vow cannot transfer what the vower never permanently held

What the shekel of the sanctuary means: Clarke takes it as a standard kept there to regulate all the weights of the land, Ellicott grounds the requirement on the proceeds going to the sanctuary's upkeep, while Gill denies that the sanctuary shekel differed from the common one and makes the point simply full weight
outliers: Ellicott notes that the man who vowed an hereditary field could pay by yearly instalments, while the purchaser of a lease paid all at once
Gill describes the seller of such a field as one in poverty and distress, obliged to sell
Wesley calls the sum paid a holy thing, consecrated to God in place of the land it redeems
Gill insists that every shekel ought to have matched the sanctuary standard

26.pericope_label: Only the firstling of the beasts no man shall sanctify; no devoted thing shall be sold or redeemed; none devoted of men shall be redeemed, but shall surely be put to death

schools.summary: Gill says the firstlings are excepted from being sanctified for the good reason given in the next clause, that they are the Lord's already. On the unclean firstling he narrows the case, holding that this is not the firstling of unclean creatures in common, which was to be redeemed with a lamb and not with money, but such as were sanctified or vowed for the reparation of the sanctuary, as Jarchi notes. He marks the difference between the two kinds of vow precisely: sanctifying and devoting were both vows, but devoting had an execration or curse added to it, by which a man imprecated a curse upon himself if what he devoted were put to any other use than that for which he devoted it, so that this sort of vow was absolute and irrevocable and what was vowed unalienable, and therefore not to be sold or redeemed, whereas things sanctified might be. On the last verse he argues from the wording twice over: it is not said, as in the preceding verse, none devoted unto the Lord, so that men devoted to ruin and destruction must be meant, for whom there was no redemption; and it is not said devoted by men but of men, that is, from among men, whether devoted by God himself, as idolaters and the nations of Canaan and especially the Amalekites, who were not to be spared on any account. Calvin adds the caution that none should offer what is already God's property, since to consecrate what is already due to him is to present stolen goods, and the ambition to lay God under obligation is almost natural to us all.

Henry treats the first exception as a caution that no man should make such a jest of sanctifying things to the Lord as to sanctify a firstling, which was God's already by the law. From this he draws a rule about vows in general: though the matter of a general vow may be that which we were before obliged to, as in our sacramental covenant, a singular vow should be of that which we were not, in such circumstances and proportions, antecedently bound to. He then sets the two categories of the chapter side by side, distinguishing things or persons devoted from things or persons that were only sanctified, and it is on that distinction that the remaining verses turn, since what is merely sanctified may be valued, redeemed and sold, while what is devoted may not.

Ellicott prefers the rendering nevertheless at both places where the particle occurs, and observes that the legislator, having laid down regulations for the four classes of objects which may be vowed, namely persons, animals, houses and lands, concludes by pointing out two exceptions to the rules hitherto discussed. Of the unclean firstling he says the owner could redeem it at the priest's valuation with a fifth added, and that if he did not, the treasurer of the sanctuary sold it to any buyer at that valuation, the proceeds going to the maintenance and repair of the sanctuary; he notes that this is at variance with the earlier law by which the firstborn of an ass was to be redeemed with a sheep or put to death. On the ban he says that, unlike the things consecrated by the vows hitherto spoken of, a banned thing cannot be redeemed, and he measures the reach of the power, since a man might ban not only his cattle and his otherwise inalienable inherited land but also the human beings over whom he had control, his children and his slaves. The banned man comes irretrievably under the class of most holy, that is, one irrevocably withdrawn from the power of man; and though he is surely to be put to death, Ellicott denies that this is as a sacrifice to God, holding rather that he is removed out of God's sight. Keil states the governing principle, that what belonged to the Lord by law could not be dedicated to him by a vow.

Wesley says the firstling may not be vowed because it is not the man's own but the Lord's already, so that to vow it is a tacit derogation from and a usurpation of the Lord's right, and a mocking of God by pretending to give what we cannot withhold from him; under ox and sheep he takes all other beasts that might be sacrificed to be comprehended, whose firstlings could not be redeemed but had to be sacrificed, whereas the firstlings of men were redeemed and so could be vowed. The unclean firstling he explains by its double disqualification, since it could not be vowed because it was a firstborn nor offered because it was unclean, and is therefore commanded to be redeemed or sold. Of the devoted thing he says it is what is absolutely devoted to God with a curse upon the vower or others if they do not dispose of it according to the vow, and that most holy means it might be touched or employed by the priests only and by no other persons, not even by their own families. On the last verse he insists that the text reads of men and not by men, so that men are here not the persons devoting but the persons devoted to destruction, whether by God's sentence upon idolaters, Canaanites and Amalekites, or by men in pursuance of such a sentence, or for some crime of a high nature; and he warns expressly that this is not to be generally understood, as if a man might by virtue of the text devote his own child. Clarke calls the ban an absolute unredeemable grant to God, and refuses the inference that the passage licenses human sacrifice.

debates: What the last verse permits: Gill and Wesley both argue from the grammar that the men in question are devoted to destruction rather than devoting, and Wesley adds that no man could by this text devote his own child; Clarke refuses the claim of the enemies of revelation that human sacrifice is licensed here, noting how obscure and brief the words are; and Ellicott, while accepting that the banned man is put to death, denies that he is offered to God, holding that he is removed out of his sight

Why the firstling may not be vowed: Keil rests it on the rule that what is the Lord's by law cannot be dedicated by vow, Calvin on the theft involved in offering what is already his, Wesley on the usurpation and mockery of pretending to give what cannot be withheld, and Henry on the difference between a general vow and a singular one

How devoting differs from sanctifying: Gill locates it in the execration attached, which makes the vow absolute and irrevocable, Clarke calls the ban an unredeemable grant, Henry sets the two categories side by side as the hinge of the chapter, and Wesley explains the resulting status as one that only priests may touch
outliers: Ellicott and Keil both note that this rule about the unclean firstling stands at variance with the earlier law of the ass redeemed by a sheep
Ellicott observes that a man might ban his own children and slaves along with his cattle and his patrimony
Gill cites Jarchi to restrict the case to firstlings vowed for the reparation of the sanctuary
Calvin says the ambition to lay God under an obligation is almost natural to us all

30.pericope_label: All the tithe of the land is the LORD’S; concerning the tithe of the herd or the flock, whatsoever passeth under the rod, the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the several sorts of tithe, the first tithe, the tithe out of the tithe, the second tithe and the poor's tithe, generally reduced to three, and cites the older testimony and Maimonides on the years in which each was separated. On the redemption he notes from Jarchi that the fifth part was added when a man redeemed his own tithes and not when he redeemed his neighbour's. He observes from the Targums that the law of the tithe of the herd concerns oxen and sheep only, since none but clean beasts were tithed, though the firstlings of unclean beasts were to be redeemed; and on the prohibition of searching he says the owner was not to consider whether the beast was in a good or bad state of health, fat or lean, perfect or blemished, but to take it as it was. The closing verse he refers either to what is contained in this chapter or rather to the whole book, delivered to Moses for the children of Israel, priests and people alike, and given near Sinai after the tabernacle was set up and the Lord spoke out of it. Calvin says that in assigning the tithes to the Levites God ceded his own rights, since they were a kind of royal revenue, and so bars all complaint from the other tribes, appointing the priests his receivers to collect in his name what could not be refused without impious and sacrilegious fraud; and he takes the last verse as commending the Law promulgated on the two tables, whose authority rests both on its being delivered by God and on Moses having been appointed rather than having assumed the office of lawgiver.

Henry takes the last verse as having reference to the whole book, and closes on the difference between what abides and what has passed. Many of the precepts in it are moral and always binding; others are ceremonial and peculiar to the Jewish nation, yet even these have a spiritual meaning and so teach us, since the gospel was preached to them by these institutions as well as to us. The doctrine of reconciliation to God by a Mediator, he says, is not clouded with the smoke of burning sacrifice but cleared by the knowledge of Christ and him crucified; and we are under the sweet and easy institutions of the gospel rather than the dark shadows of the law.

Ellicott names the tithes as the last of the things which cannot be dedicated to the Lord by a vow, since, like the firstborn of animals, they already belong to God by another statute, so that a man cannot vow to God what is not his own; the tithe of the land he takes of the soil and what grows on it, in distinction from the tithe of the herd mentioned later. On the redemption he observes that a man may still redeem his tithes by adding one-fifth to their actual value, while by the rule of the second Temple anyone was allowed to redeem the tithes due from another person by paying the exact value without the fifth, the tithes then being eaten in any place while the redemption money had to be taken to Jerusalem. He quotes the Jewish canonists at length on the passing under the rod, that the owner gathers his lambs or calves into the fold and makes a little door so that two cannot go out at once, placing the dams outside, so that as they bleat the young hear their voices and go out to meet them, since the beast must pass of itself and not be brought out; and on the prohibition of searching he says the owner is not to pick out the good from the bad but to mark every tenth as it comes from the fold. Keil sets down the rule that no discrimination was to be made between good and bad and no exchange, and that if an exchange were made both animals became holy.

Clarke says God claims the tithe of the land as his own, and speaks of it as a point perfectly settled about which there was neither doubt nor difficulty, referring the reader to his own earlier treatment rather than adding to it. He gives the rabbinic account of the tithing of cattle at length: when a man was to give the tithe of his sheep or calves, he shut the whole flock into one fold with a narrow door capable of letting out one at a time, and stood by the door with a rod whose end was dipped in vermilion or red ochre, the mothers standing without; the door being opened, the young ran out to join their dams, and every tenth was marked as it passed. Of the closing verse he observes that the conclusion is very similar to that at the end of the preceding chapter, and repeats his supposition that this chapter should have followed the twenty-fifth and that the twenty-sixth originally terminated the book; he ends with Ainsworth's reflection on the tithes being sanctified to God's honour, the maintenance of his ministers and the relief of the poor. Wesley takes the tithe here of the ordinary and yearly tithes belonging to the Levites, as the expression intimates and the addition of the fifth in case of redemption implies, and leaves open whether the rod is the tither's, since the Jews drove their cattle through a narrow passage where the tenth was marked and reserved for the priest, or the shepherd's, under which the herds passed and by which they were governed and numbered.

debates: What the tithe of the land covers: Ellicott takes it of the soil and its produce as distinct from the tithe of the herd, Gill distinguishes the several tithes of Jewish practice and their years, and Wesley confines the reference to the ordinary yearly tithe of the Levites, arguing from the very provision for redemption

Whose rod is meant: Clarke and Ellicott both give the rabbinic scene of the narrow door and the marking rod and take it of the tither's, Ellicott adding the canonists' rule that the beast must pass of itself, while Wesley leaves the choice open between the tither's rod and the shepherd's, under which the flocks were numbered

What the closing verse refers to: Gill takes it either of this chapter or rather of the whole book, Ellicott of the laws of this chapter only, Clarke uses it to renew his conjecture that the chapter is out of place and that the preceding one once ended the book, while Henry and Wesley refer it to the book entire and turn it into a contrast between the shadows of the law and the light of the gospel
outliers: Calvin says God ceded his own rights in giving the tithes to the Levites, since they were a kind of royal revenue
Ellicott records that a man might redeem another's tithes without the added fifth, though the money had to be carried to Jerusalem
Clarke repeats his conjecture that this chapter belongs after the twenty-fifth
Gill notes from the Targums that only clean beasts, oxen and sheep, were tithed
